ELLISVILLE – Two people were arrested after Jones County Sheriff’s Department narcotics agents executed a search warrant overnight Monday at a house near Ellisville, according to Sheriff Joe Berlin.

Authorities said narcotics agents, along with patrol deputies and criminal investigators, served the warrant at 69 Mrs. Robinson Road.

Arrested at the scene were 57-year-old William Stewart and 45-year-old Karen Clark, the sheriff’s department said.

Stewart was charged with possession of a controlled substance, methamphetamine, and also had an outstanding Mississippi Department of Corrections warrant, according to authorities.

Clark was charged with possession of a controlled substance with intent to distribute, methamphetamine, the sheriff’s department said.

Agents seized about 28 grams of methamphetamine from Clark and about 3 grams from Stewart.

“These arrests are a direct result of information gained by JCSD Narcotics Division agents including Sergeant Chase Smith, Corporal Dalton Ainsworth, and Agent Jamey Beard,” Berlin said in a statement.

Berlin also issued a warning to people selling illegal drugs in the county.

“We keep making it clear that if you are selling illegal narcotics in Jones County that we are coming to visit,” Berlin said. “Check that ‘going to jail’ box once again and see you soon.”

Both Stewart and Clark were being held at the Jones County Adult Detention Facility pending their initial appearance in Jones County Justice Court.

PEARL — State leaders gathered Tuesday to cut the ribbon on the new Mississippi Department of Public Safety headquarters in Pearl, a multimillion-dollar facility designed to bring all major public safety divisions under one roof for the first time.

The approximately 146,000-square-foot complex consolidates agencies including the Highway Safety Patrol, Bureau of Investigation, Bureau of Narcotics and Office of Homeland Security, with the goal of improving coordination and efficiency across state law enforcement operations.

Speaking at the ceremony, Governor Tate Reeves called the building “an investment in the people who help keep our state safe,” while emphasizing his administration’s continued support for law enforcement.

“In Mississippi, we back the blue,” Reeves said. “That is not just a slogan, it is a commitment. It’s a promise that we will stand with law enforcement just as you stand for us.”

Reeves said the facility represents years of planning and legislative support, noting that major state investments like the new headquarters require cooperation across branches of government.

Public Safety Commissioner Sean Tindell described the opening as a “milestone moment” late in his tenure, saying the agency is already operating inside the building as final components are moved in.

The new headquarters comes after a legislative session that included tensions between lawmakers and first responders, but Tindell said Mississippi’s support for law enforcement remains strong.

“The commitment’s been there for a long time, and Mississippi does support the blue,” he said. “This is a great building … but the greatest asset that we have in this state is our state employees, especially our first responders on the front lines.”

The facility was designed to improve collaboration between divisions through shared space and proximity, with officials saying the move is expected to enhance communication and operational effectiveness.

State leaders said the investment reflects ongoing efforts to strengthen public safety infrastructure as Mississippi continues to address issues such as crime, drug trafficking and emergency response.

Officials said the building will serve as the central hub for DPS operations moving forward, marking a significant step in modernizing the state’s public safety system.

Tindell also addressed questions about the agency’s former headquarters site on Woodrow Wilson Avenue in Jackson, where lawmakers are considering future use of the property.

“That’s obviously a very premier corner in the state of Mississippi,” Tindell said, adding that he expects the Legislature “will ultimately pick a good future use for it that meets the demands for the citizens of the state.”

WIGGINS – An 18-wheeler collided with a train Friday afternoon at a railroad crossing in Wiggins before leaving the scene, according to the Wiggins Fire Department.

Firefighters responded at about 1 p.m. to the crossing on South 1st Street between East Fifth Avenue and Mill Avenue after reports of a crash involving a train and a tractor-trailer.

When crews arrived, the train was stopped on the tracks and showed no visible damage, according to the fire department.

According to the train crew, the 18-wheeler crossed the tracks without stopping, and the train’s engine struck the rear portion of the trailer.

The truck left the scene before emergency responders arrived.

The Wiggins Police Department later located and stopped the 18-wheeler. The driver reported no injuries, according to the fire department.

Minor injuries were reported among members of the train crew, but no one needed to be taken by ambulance.

The crash remains under investigation by local law enforcement and other appropriate authorities.

The Wiggins Fire Department reminded drivers to come to a complete stop at all railroad crossings and look both ways before proceeding.

RIDGELAND — The City of Ridgeland is pleased to announce the appointment of Paul Forster, City Engineer, as its representative on the newly established Metro Jackson Water Authority Board. Forster will serve as a member-at-large, appointed by Mayor Gene McGee and confirmed by the Board of Aldermen.

The Metro Jackson Water Authority, created through the Metro Jackson Water Authority Act, is expected to assume oversight of Jackson’s water and sewer systems following the conclusion of the current federal receivership. The nine-member governing board will include appointments from multiple jurisdictions, including the City of Jackson, the Governor’s Office, the Lieutenant Governor, and the mayors of Ridgeland and Byram.

Forster brings extensive experience in civil engineering and public service. Prior to joining Ridgeland, Forster served as City Engineer and Director of Engineering and Utilities for the City of Flowood, and now serves as Ridgeland’s City Engineer. In that role, he oversaw a wide range of operations including utility management, capital improvement planning, construction oversight, budgeting, personnel management, and regulatory compliance.

In his role with the City, Forster supports key areas including transportation, water and sewer infrastructure, environmental initiatives, and community development, ensuring the City continues to meet the demands of growth while maintaining high standards of service. Mr. Forster has extensive experience in utility management, capital improvement planning, construction oversight, budgeting, personnel management, and regulatory compliance. He also serves on the Commission for the City of Jackson 1% Special Sales Tax.

“We are looking forward to serving the entirety of the jurisdiction on this authority, and we hope to contribute to the success of the entire metro area through our efforts,” said Forster.

The City of Ridgeland looks forward to supporting the Metro Jackson Water Authority and working collaboratively with regional partners to strengthen water and wastewater services for the entire community.

CLAIBORNE COUNTY — The Claiborne County Sheriff’s Department is warning parents about a popular high school game known as “Senior Assassin,” saying the activity can create dangerous misunderstandings and potential public safety risks.

In a statement, the department said it has received reports that local students are participating in the game, which often involves using water guns or similar items to “target” other players. Deputies cautioned that, despite its intended harmless nature, the activity can appear threatening to bystanders.

“While this activity may seem harmless, it can create the very real appearance of someone being targeted or ‘gunned down,’ especially in today’s climate,” the department said, urging parents to contact their children and stop participation.

The warning echoes concerns raised by law enforcement agencies nationwide as the game has gained popularity among high school seniors. According to Parents.com, participants are typically assigned a target and attempt to “eliminate” them using water guns or balloons, often outside of school in public spaces like neighborhoods and parks.

Authorities say the use of realistic-looking toy guns or disguises, such as masks, can alarm the public and lead to emergency responses. In one case cited by Good Morning America, police responded to a report of an armed individual, only to discover a teen playing the game with what appeared to be a real firearm. The teen was arrested and faced felony charges after officers determined the weapon was a water gun that closely resembled a handgun.

Other incidents have escalated even further. In Louisiana, a homeowner fired warning shots after mistaking teens hiding with toy guns for potential intruders, highlighting how quickly the game can turn dangerous, according to Good Morning America reporting.

Experts say the risks go beyond confusion. Parents.com reports that realistic toy weapons have, in some cases, led to fatal encounters when mistaken for real firearms, underscoring the potential consequences of the activity.

Law enforcement officials are encouraging families to have open conversations with their children about the risks, set clear boundaries and emphasize safety.

The Claiborne County Sheriff’s Department stressed that parents are ultimately responsible for their children’s actions and warned that participation could lead to serious consequences.

“Let’s work together to keep our community safe and avoid a situation that could quickly get out of hand,” the department said.

GULF COAST — Amtrak’s Mardi Gras Service, which restored passenger rail to the Mississippi Gulf Coast last August, reached 100,000 riders in just eight months — well ahead of the 71,000 passengers the rail company had projected for its first full year of operation.

The milestone, announced by U.S. Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., comes as the route has earned the highest passenger satisfaction rating of any Amtrak service in the country. Demand has been strong enough that Amtrak added weekend capacity to accommodate travelers.

The service, which launched Aug. 16, 2025, restored a rail connection that the Gulf Coast had been without for nearly 20 years following Hurricane Katrina.

“The Gulf Coast waited nearly 20 years for the return of passenger rail, and they have given the Mardi Gras Service a warm welcome,” Wicker said in a statement.

Wicker, the former chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, spent roughly a decade pushing for the route’s revival. His efforts included securing more than $200 million in federal funding, pressing Transportation Department nominees on their commitment to Gulf Coast rail, and testifying before the Surface Transportation Board in 2022 to advocate for Amtrak’s application to restore service.

A 2015 surface transportation law Wicker shepherded through the Commerce Committee created a Gulf Coast Working Group to study whether passenger rail should return to the region — the first time passenger rail funding was included in such a reauthorization bill.

Wicker said he expects the service to continue generating economic benefits for Mississippi and neighboring Gulf states.

JACKSON – The Mississippi Court of Appeals denied a request on Tuesday by the Hinds County School District to reconsider its ruling that a former elementary school administrator was wrongfully fired for reading a children’s book about flatulence to second graders.

The court denied the rehearing motion without comment in the case of Toby Price v. Hinds County School District.

Price, a former assistant principal at Gary Road Elementary School, was terminated by the Hinds County School Board after he read “I Need a New Butt!” to approximately 240 second graders on Read Across America Day.

The school board upheld Superintendent Stephanie Martin’s decision to fire Price, citing five reasons including that the book contained nudity and inappropriate illustrations, that Price had shown poor professional judgment, that the reading negatively affected at least one student, that Price violated the Mississippi Code of Ethics, and that Price lacked credibility as a witness.

Hinds County Chancery Court Judge Tiffany Grove upheld the board’s decision in July 2024, writing that while she was “sympathetic to Mr. Price’s circumstances of termination for a single instance of admittedly poor judgment,” the board’s decision was supported by substantial evidence and she lacked authority to substitute her judgment for the board’s.

The Court of Appeals reversed that ruling, finding the board’s decision was not supported by substantial evidence and was arbitrary and capricious. The appeals court found no “stark contrast” between the book Price read and other books already in the school’s library, several of which also contained references to nudity or the word “butt.”

The school district then filed a motion for rehearing, arguing the appeals court had improperly substituted its judgment for the school board’s, failed to address all five reasons for termination, and misread the legal standard governing appeals of school board decisions.

The district’s attorneys argued that under Mississippi precedent, a board’s termination decision should stand if even one valid reason supports it, and contended the court had ignored Price’s own admission that he had used “poor judgment.”

Price’s attorney, Joel Dillard, opposed the rehearing request, calling it “a fairly wholesale recapitulation” of arguments the court had already considered. Dillard argued the book’s content and the board’s allowance of similar materials in the school library made the case straightforward.

The court’s denial of rehearing leaves the appeals court’s ruling in favor of Price in place. It is unclear whether the school district intends to seek further review from the Mississippi Supreme Court.
https://darkhorsepressnow.com/news/2026-.summary: JACKSON – The Mississippi Court of Appeals denied a request on Tuesday by the Hinds County School District to reconsider its ruling that a former elementary school administrator was wrongfully fired for reading a children’s book about flatulence to second graders.

JACKSON — Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch announced Tuesday the distribution of nearly $1.5 million to nine organizations serving human trafficking victims across the state, bringing the total awarded from a dedicated state fund to $11 million since its creation in 2020.

The grants come from the Victims of Human Trafficking and Commercial Sexual Exploitation Fund, which the Legislature established in 2020 to support direct service providers working with trafficking victims.

The largest award, $441,507, went to the Center for Violence Prevention to expand support services statewide through its Tower residential program and a Rapid Response Team of advocates. The Domestic Abuse Family Shelter received $283,134 to serve victims across an 11-county area, and the Gulf Coast Center for Nonviolence received $241,219 for holistic services to individuals and families affected by trafficking.

Southern Christian Services received $239,215 to continue operating what the attorney general’s office described as Mississippi’s only safe home exclusively for adolescent trafficking survivors, where young people can receive therapeutic services for up to two years.

The Mississippi Coalition Against Human Trafficking received $161,608 for its Independent Living Assistance Program, which connects survivors with mentoring, financial planning, and case management for up to 18 months. Easterseals received $51,236 for education and awareness efforts in Lee and Pontotoc counties, and the Southwest Mississippi Children’s Advocacy Center received $38,502 for mental health therapy services.

Smaller awards went to Sunnybrook Children’s Home, which received $7,198, and Hope Community Collective, which received $3,000 for a bilingual family support advocate.

The funding was delayed after Gov. Tate Reeves vetoed a $2.5 million appropriation during a 2025 special legislative session. The Legislature approved $1.5 million during the 2026 regular session, allowing the fund committee to complete partial awards it had announced in December.

The fund is financed through court assessments from certain criminal convictions, donations, and legislative appropriations.

JACKSON — On Earth Day, Mississippi leaders and conservation advocates are encouraging residents to step outside and explore the landscapes that have long defined the state’s identity.

From winding rivers and cypress-filled bayous to pine forests and rolling hills, Mississippi’s outdoors tell a story of ecosystems that have shaped communities and sustained generations. The Great Mississippi Nature Trail brings many of those landscapes together, offering access to natural areas, state parks, wildlife refuges and scenic trails across the state.

The trail connects destinations ranging from waterfalls and rail trails to quiet wilderness areas, showcasing Mississippi’s ecological diversity and cultural history.

“Happy Earth Day,” the Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce posted on Facebook Wednesday. “There’s no better time to celebrate Native Plant Month than by getting outside and discovering the beauty of Mississippi’s natural landscape.”

When most people think of Mississippi, they picture the Delta, the blues, or the Mississippi River itself. But tucked along the Great Mississippi Nature Trail is a botanical world full of carnivorous plants, ancient cypress groves, and some of the most diverse native flora in the entire country.

If you’re interested in a starting point, go with Crosby Arboretum in Picayune. This 104-acre native plant conservatory is home to more than 700 species of trees, shrubs, wildflowers, and grasses, and that’s just the interpretive center. Wander into the pitcher plant bogs and you’ll find yourself face to face with some of nature’s most clever survivors. Sundews have a sticky “dew” designed to trap unsuspecting insects. Parrot pitcher plants, which are compact little carnivorous plants only four to six inches tall, sit quietly waiting for their next meal.

Head north and watch the landscape shift noticeably. At Leroy Percy State Park, huge oaks draped in Spanish moss frame artesian springs that have been flowing for centuries. At Tishomingo State Park, swamp cypress trees line Bear Creek against a backdrop of sandstone bluffs.

In the Delta, the Yazoo National Wildlife Refuge and Delta National Forest tell a different story: one of bottomland hardwoods, where oak, ash, elm, and cottonwood form a canopy that supports white-tailed deer, wild turkey, and hundreds of migratory bird species.

What ties all of these places together is Mississippi’s extensive plant diversity. The state is home to roughly 200 native tree species alone, from longleaf pine in the piney woods of the south to hardwood forests in the north. Some of the rarest plants in the country — bog flax, bog spicebush, and native orchids — cling to existence in the Gulf Coast’s wet pine savannas, where less than 3% of the original habitat remains.

The Great Mississippi Nature Trail is a chance to see the state’s wild side before it disappears. Officials said the trail provides opportunities for all types of visitors, whether they are planning a family outing, a scenic drive or a weekend on the water.

Popular stops along the route include state parks such as LeFleur’s Bluff State Park, Tishomingo State Park and Percy Quin State Park, as well as federal sites like the Natchez Trace Parkway and the Noxubee National Wildlife Refuge. Local favorites such as the Longleaf Trace and unique natural landmarks like Red Bluff also draw visitors each year.

Advocates say spending time outdoors is not only a way to celebrate Earth Day, but also a way to build a deeper connection to the environment.

The Department of Agriculture and Commerce encouraged Mississippians to explore areas where native plants thrive, noting that understanding local ecosystems can help residents make more sustainable choices at home.

For those planning a trip, officials recommend bringing plenty of water, checking trail conditions ahead of time and following “Leave No Trace” principles to protect natural resources. Spring and fall are often considered the best times to visit, offering milder weather and increased wildlife activity. Activities along the trail range from hiking and fishing to kayaking and wildlife viewing, with many sites designed to accommodate families through accessible boardwalks and rail trails.

As Earth Day underscores the importance of conservation, leaders say Mississippi’s natural spaces remain both a resource and a responsibility.

By exploring the state’s outdoors, they say, residents can better appreciate the landscapes that make Mississippi unique and help ensure they are preserved for future generations.
